I have 3.8 mu of land here in Quzhou, and after six years I know what this soil can do. With five people in my household but only me and my husband working the land most days — our son and daughter-in-law have jobs in the county town — I cannot afford crops that demand too much labor all at once. That is why I keep chili as my main crop: it brings the best cash income per mu, and the buyers from Shijiazhuang and Handan come right to our village to purchase. But I also need maize for our own food and for the pigs we raise, so I always set aside part of the land for that.

It is mid-April now, and the soil temperature is finally rising. This week I will rotary till the entire field to break up the clods and level the ground. I am putting 2.5 mu into chili. I will buy hybrid chili seedlings from the market in town — I learned my lesson four years ago when traditional seed gave me poor disease resistance and I lost money. Hybrids cost more upfront, but they withstand the viral diseases and root rot that strike when our summer turns humid. Before transplanting, I will spread compound fertilizer as a base, and when the plants start flowering in June I will top-dress with urea and potassium fertilizer. Chili is greedy for nutrients and water, especially during flowering and fruit swelling, so I will irrigate eight times using my well. The well is everything — two years ago we had a dry June and neighbors without wells saw their flowers drop. I also know the aphids and mites will come by July, so I will spray pesticides six times, watching carefully for the first sign of spots or curling leaves. If the weather cooperates, I expect about 2,800 kg per mu of fresh red peppers.

The remaining 1.3 mu I will plant with hybrid maize. Spring maize does not need the constant attention that chili demands, which suits me because August is when the chili harvest peaks and I cannot be everywhere at once. I will apply base fertilizer at sowing and top-dress once when the stalks are knee-high. Four irrigations will be enough — at sowing, jointing, tasseling, and grain-filling. Two pesticide applications will control corn borer, which is the main threat here. I expect around 520 kg per mu, which will fill our grain jar and leave some for the animals.

This is my plan every year: let the chili bring in cash, let the maize feed the family, and use the well to make sure drought does not ruin us. I keep the chili area at 2.5 mu because that is the most I can manage well with the labor I have. Better to do a thorough job on 2.5 mu than to do poorly on more.
